The original proposed rulemaking issued in 2002 sought to create an exception to
the enhanced due diligence requirement for those offshore banks that were branches of
well-regulated foreign banks. Specifically, we proposed to exclude from enhanced due
diligence those foreign banks operating under an offshore banking license that are
branches of banks licensed in a jurisdiction where one or more banks had been
determined by the Federal Reserve to be subject to comprehensive supervision or
regulation on a consolidated basis. The notice of proposed rulemaking issued today takes
a different approach, focusing instead on clarifying that U.S. financial institutions have
some flexibility in applying the enhanced due diligence procedures on a risk-assessed
basis, tailoring the enhanced due diligence to the risks associated with the particular
account. Comments are sought on all aspects of this proposed rulemaking.
II. Private Banking Provisions
The final rule requires certain U.S. financial institutions to establish and maintain
a due diligence program for private banking accounts that is reasonably designed to
detect and report any known or suspected money laundering or suspicious activity.
Included in this requirement is the duty to conduct enhanced scrutiny of any private
banking account that is maintained for senior foreign political figures, their immediate

Box B.14. Code of ethics of an umbrella NPO organisation based in Canada

encompasses a statement of principles of development as well as a code of conduct,
and outlines the ethical principles that must be adhered to, and promoted, by the
organisation and its members. Below is an excerpt from the Code related to
organisational integrity:
Governance
 Each Organisation shall be governed fairly and responsibly by an
independent, active and informed governing body (e.g., the Board of
Directors).

except for reasonable expenses incurred to fulfil their organisational duties.

numeric.question: Compute the escalation rate of wires to any newly-added payee.
numeric.calculation:
1) Identify wires to newly-added payee Robert Johnson: amounts 2,893.15; 9,958.81; 24,006.18; 88,578.88 from transactions[0..3].
2) Compute escalation rate as last wire amount divided by first wire amount: 88,578.88 / 2,893.15 = 30.6129 from transactions[0] and transactions[3].
3) Round to two decimals: 30.61.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: No. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires suspicious activity reporting by a financial institution, and the facts do not show a covered financial institution or a reporting failure.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that a financial institution (as defined/covered under the BSA framework) report suspicious transactions to the government and provides related protections (e.g., safe harbor and confidentiality). Element-by-element: (1) Covered actor: § 5318(g) applies to a “financial institution” and its SAR obligations; the fact pattern describes an individual customer (SYN_4a4c637a) sending wires, but does not identify the involved bank/MSB/other covered financial institution or its compliance duties. (2) Triggering suspicious transaction: the wires (including large amounts and activity inconsistent with the stated expected monthly volume and a newly-added payee) could be suspicious, but § 5318(g) is about the institution’s reporting requirement, not the customer’s conduct. (3) Reporting/violation: the facts do not state whether any financial institution filed or failed to file a SAR. Therefore, it cannot be determined whether § 5318(g) applies on these facts. Contiguous phrase in answer and here: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires suspicious activity reporting”.
